disease-biology|d. melanogaster.summary: Zong et al. 2023 found modest within-stage transcriptome similarity between D. melanogaster and C. elegans (most genome-wide c-scores >0.1; ce.lar–dm.lar c-score = 0.087). The study reports no direct D. melanogaster–human disease comparisons, so evidence is insufficient to judge tracking of human disease.
key_numbers: most genome-wide c-scores >0.1 (within-stage D. melanogaster–C. elegans)
ce.lar–dm.lar c-score = 0.087

disease-biology|pig.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: swine thrombin generation partly tracked human values (peak 242.35 nM vs 484.25; rate 93.6 vs 111.51 nM/min) but swine had no detectable plasmin while humans showed plasmin peak 457.2 nM and rate 34.8 nM/min. Thus swine reflect thrombin but not plasmin/fibrinolysis.
key_numbers: Thrombin peak: 242.35 nM (swine) vs 484.25 nM (human)
Thrombin production rate: 93.6 nM/min (swine) vs 111.51 nM/min (human)
Plasmin peak: not detected (swine) vs 457.2 nM (human)
Plasmin production rate: not detected (swine) vs 34.8 nM/min (human)

disease-biology|c. elegans.summary: Evidence shows modest cross-species transcriptomic concordance for C. elegans with Drosophila: genome-wide c-scores >0.1 for most within-stage comparisons, though one pair (ce.lar–dm.lar) was 0.087. The study reports no direct C. elegans–human disease concordance.
key_numbers: genome-wide c-scores >0.1 for most within-stage Drosophila–C. elegans comparisons
c-score = 0.087 for C. elegans larva–Drosophila larva (ce.lar–dm.lar)
disease-biology|c. elegans.why_range_is_wide: Variation comes from different developmental stage pairs (some within-stage pairs exceeded 0.1 while ce.lar–dm.lar was 0.087).

disease-biology|rabbit.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: Rabbit thrombin generation was much lower than in humans (peak 71.6 nM = 15% of human 484.3; rate 14.9 nM/min = 13% of human 111.5), while plasmin measures were closer (peak 197.7 nM = 43%; rate 17.6 = 51%). Rabbit plasmin-generation curves were highly variable.
key_numbers: Thrombin peak 71.6 nM (15% of human 484.25 nM)
Thrombin production rate 14.93 nM/min (13% of human 111.51 nM)
Plasmin peak 197.71 nM (43% of human 457.20 nM)
Plasmin production rate 17.63 nM/min (51% of human 34.80 nM)
disease-biology|rabbit.why_range_is_wide: Rabbit plasmin-generation (PG) curves showed high variability.

disease-biology|horse.summary: Oreff et al. 2021: Horse tenocyte transcriptomes resembled human under transient inflammation (Mahalanobis 9.59 vs 23.05 in healthy), and proliferation difference was small/non-significant under transient inflammation (slope 0.0233, p=0.49). Migration differed from human in healthy (slope 0.0133, p=0.0038) and constant inflammation (−0.014, p=0.0302).
key_numbers: Mahalanobis distance to human (all genes): transient inflammation 9.59
Mahalanobis distance to human (all genes): healthy 23.05
Proliferation slope difference vs human: transient inflammation 0.0233 (p=0.4868)
Migration slope difference vs human: healthy 0.0132563 (p=0.00375)
Migration slope difference vs human: constant inflammation −0.0140 (p=0.0302)
disease-biology|horse.why_range_is_wide: Similarity and functional measures change with inflammatory state (healthy vs transient vs constant), producing the varied distances and slope differences.

disease-biology|mouse.summary: Evidence is mixed: some studies report very low transcript concordance (Seok et al. R^2 ≤ 0.09; Kodamullil et al. mice mimicked 12% of human‑deregulated genes), while others find moderate/strong agreement (Takao et al. Spearman 0.43–0.68 with 77–93% directional concordance; Holland et al. recall 0.40). Concordance depends on disease/model, analysis thresholds and exposure duration.
key_numbers: R^2 ≤ 0.09 — correlation of gene expression changes between human conditions and mouse orthologs (4,918 human genes)
Spearman 0.43–0.68 — rank correlation of gene fold-changes between human conditions and mouse models (Takao et al. 2015)
77–93% — % of genes changing in same direction between human and mouse (Takao et al. 2015)
12% — proportion of human-deregulated genes mimicked by mouse models (Kodamullil et al. 2017)
0.40 — recall of genes altered in human liver disease detected by 12‑month CCl4 mouse model (Holland et al. 2022)
disease-biology|mouse.why_range_is_wide: Estimates vary by disease/model, data-processing thresholds (fold‑change/P-value), and experiment duration/exposure.

disease-biology|non-human primate.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: baboon and rhesus thrombin measures approximated human values (thrombin peak 433.8 and 399.0 nM vs human 484.3; production rates 124.2 and 111.2 nM/min vs human 111.5). Plasmin peaks were higher (546–566 vs 457 nM) and plasmin production rate was markedly higher in baboon (90.8 vs 34.8 nM/min).
key_numbers: Thrombin peak: baboon 433.78 nM, rhesus 398.95 nM vs human 484.25 nM
Thrombin production rate: baboon 124.22 nM/min, rhesus 111.22 nM/min vs human 111.51 nM/min
Plasmin peak: baboon 546.26 nM, rhesus 565.84 nM vs human 457.20 nM
Plasmin production rate: baboon 90.81 nM/min, rhesus 49.78 nM/min vs human 34.80 nM/min
disease-biology|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Different metrics diverge: thrombin measures are close to human while plasmin production rates are substantially higher (especially in baboon).

disease-biology|rat.summary: Rats partially recapitulate human disease biology: 26/30 blood biochemical changes after exercise matched humans and only 1/19 biomarkers showed a species×exercise interaction (Goutianos et al. 2015; Veskoukis et al. 2016). However concordance is system-dependent—coagulation peaks were lower in rats (thrombin 270 nM vs 484 nM; plasmin 186 vs 457 nM, Tarandovskiy et al. 2020) and whole-transcriptome alignment was ≈50% though some diet models scored MHPS=0.941 (Vacca et al. 2024).
key_numbers: 26/30 blood biochemical variables changed toward the same direction after exercise (Goutianos et al. 2015)
1/19 biomarkers showed a species×exercise interaction (Veskoukis et al. 2016)
Thrombin peak—rat 270 nM vs human 484 nM (Tarandovskiy et al. 2020)
Plasmin peak—rat 186 nM vs human 457 nM (Tarandovskiy et al. 2020)
Whole-transcriptome alignment ≈50%; MHPS up to 0.941 for CDAA-fed rats (Vacca et al. 2024)
disease-biology|rat.why_range_is_wide: Concordance varies by biological system and analysis type (whole transcriptome vs significant DEGs) and by specific disease model/diet (e.g., Western-diet vs choline-deficient).

disease-biology|sheep.summary: Oreff et al. 2021: sheep tenocyte transcriptomes match human differently by inflammation — Mahalanobis 24.78 (healthy), 10.62 (transient), 8.94 (constant), so sheep best approximate humans under constant inflammation. Proliferation/migration slope differences vs human were small (range −0.0878 to 0.1169) though some were significant.
key_numbers: Mahalanobis 24.78 (healthy)
Mahalanobis 10.62 (transient)
Mahalanobis 8.94 (constant)
proliferation/migration slope range −0.0878 to 0.1169
disease-biology|sheep.why_range_is_wide: Similarity measures differ across the three inflammatory states tested (healthy vs transient vs constant).

efficacy|non-rodent.summary: No direct efficacy data; Leenaars et al. 2019 reports toxicity concordance instead, finding non‑rodent–human concordance for liver effects 40% (n=951). The study also reports 48% of adverse drug reactions were predictable from animal data (n=221) and notes predictivity higher for non‑rodents than rodents.
key_numbers: 40% non‑rodent–human concordance for liver effects (n=951 compounds)
48% of adverse drug reactions predictable from animal data (n=221 human toxicity events)

efficacy|mouse.summary: Mixed evidence: Spanagel 2017 reports three alcoholism drugs translated from rodent models (acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene) and consistent opioid-blockade effects in mice/rats; Pan et al. 2020 finds mouse tumor TGI does not predict approval (median 0.74 vs 0.77; AUC 0.45). Pan et al. cautions few approved drugs and TGI heterogeneity may limit inference.
key_numbers: 3 drugs translated (acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene)
median TGI approved 0.74 (0–1 scale)
median TGI failed 0.77 (0–1 scale)
AUC for TGI predicting approval 0.45
ORs for higher vs lowest TGI quartiles 0.84, 0.90, 0.74 (all <1)

efficacy|non-human primate.summary: NHP drug-vs-food choice studies partially track human efficacy: d-amphetamine reduced cocaine choice in both humans and NHPs, but KOR antagonists and buspirone did not attenuate cocaine/methamphetamine/heroin choice. Females showed greater cocaine preference than males.
key_numbers: 1 drug (d-amphetamine) showed concordant attenuation of cocaine choice in NHPs and humans
≥2 drug classes (KOR antagonists; buspirone) failed to attenuate drug-vs-food choice in NHPs
1 reported sex effect: female NHPs preferred cocaine over the alternative more than males
efficacy|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Results differ by drug class, substance (stimulant vs opioid), and acute versus repeated dosing.

efficacy|sheep.summary: Perel et al. 2007: in ewe models antenatal corticosteroids increased neonatal mortality (pooled OR 12.5, 95% CI 1.9–79.2), so sheep results did not match human trials (no benefit). The estimate is very imprecise (wide CI).
efficacy|sheep.direction: evidence does not favour the model
key_numbers: 12.5 (95% CI 1.9–79.2) — pooled OR for neonatal mortality in ewe models with antenatal corticosteroids
efficacy|sheep.why_range_is_wide: The wide confidence interval reflects imprecision from small numbers/few ewe studies.

efficacy|rat.summary: Rat efficacy findings are mixed: some rat-based results translated (three medications—acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene—and the incubation of drug‑seeking seen later in smokers, alcoholics, and cocaine addicts), but other rat‑effective agents failed clinically. Concordance depends on drug class and endpoint (e.g., 2 CRH‑R1 antagonists, KOR antagonists and buspirone failed; d‑amphetamine matched).
key_numbers: 3 medications translated to clinic (acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene)
Incubation phenomenon observed in humans across 3 groups (smokers, alcoholics, cocaine addicts)
2 CRH‑R1 antagonists failed in clinical trials
d‑amphetamine showed concordant results vs KOR antagonists and buspirone which did not
efficacy|rat.why_range_is_wide: Concordance varies by drug class and outcome (behavioral vs neurochemical): some neurochemical markers and certain medications translate, while several antagonist classes failed clinically.

efficacy|rodent.summary: Rodent efficacy studies often report positive effects—62% of focal and 70% of global ischemia experiments were superior to control (O'Collins et al. 2006), and several clinical drug classes reproduced benefits in rodents (Sembach et al. 2021). However, translation is inconsistent: reported translation rates spanned 0–100% (Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022) and rodent→human concordance for liver effects was 44% (Leenaars et al. 2019).
key_numbers: 62% — focal ischemia experiments superior to control (O'Collins et al. 2006)
70% — global ischemia experiments superior to control (O'Collins et al. 2006)
0–100% — reported translation rates from animal to human studies (Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022)
44% — concordance of rodent vs human liver effects (Leenaars et al. 2019)
efficacy|rodent.why_range_is_wide: Range reflects heterogeneity across interventions, models, outcomes and likely selective reporting/publication bias noted by the authors.

safety-pharmacology|non-human primate.summary: Evidence shows NHP cardiovascular safety signals generally tracked human outcomes: Bhatt et al. 2019 reported large-animal→human combined BP/HR sensitivity 78% and specificity 79%; Sadko et al. 2024 found moxifloxacin QTc ≈10.9 ms in NHP vs ~10 ms in humans. Caveat: HR-only sensitivity 54%, PPV 52%, and predictive values depend on prevalence.
key_numbers: 78% — sensitivity for combined BP/HR (large animal→human)
79% — specificity for combined BP/HR (large animal→human)
52% — positive predictive value for combined BP/HR (large animal→human)
54% — sensitivity for HR-only (large animal→human)
10.9 ms — QTc increase in NHP (moxifloxacin) vs ~10 ms in humans

safety-pharmacology|dog.summary: Dog safety-pharmacology generally tracked human outcomes: Pollard et al. 2017 reported dog QTc AUC ≈0.81 (0.91 excluding β2‑agonists); Valentin et al. 2022 found 91% of human QT‑prolongers were positive in animals; Bhatt et al. 2019 found combined BP/HR sensitivity 78% and specificity 79%. Main qualification: Valentin also reported 31% overall discordance and performance varied by assay and drug class.
key_numbers: AUC 0.81 — concordance dog QTc vs clinical QTc (Pollard et al. 2017; 0.91 excluding β2‑agonists)
91% — of human QT‑prolonging drugs were positive in animals (Valentin et al. 2022)
31% — overall discordant drugs (Valentin et al. 2022)
Sensitivity 78% / Specificity 79% — dog to human concordance for combined BP and HR (Bhatt et al. 2019)
safety-pharmacology|dog.why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by assay, endpoint and drug class (e.g., excluding β2‑agonists raised AUC from 0.81 to 0.91).

safety-pharmacology|rat.summary: Bhatt et al. 2019 found rat signals tracked large-animal combined BP+HR reasonably (sensitivity 84%, specificity 71%, PPV 90%, NPV 60%) but were weaker for individual endpoints (BP specificity 59%, HR sensitivity 64%) and 23–26% showed opposite-direction changes. Authors note predictive values depend on dataset prevalence, which may be lower than real-world.
key_numbers: 84% sensitivity (rat→large-animal, combined BP+HR)
71% specificity (rat→large-animal, combined BP+HR)
90% PPV (rat→large-animal, combined BP+HR)
60% NPV (rat→large-animal, combined BP+HR)
23–26% opposite direction (rat→large-animal; HR 23%, BP 26%)
safety-pharmacology|rat.why_range_is_wide: Performance differs between combined BP+HR analyses (higher concordance) and individual BP or HR analyses; some measures also had opposite-direction changes.

toxicology|rabbit.summary: Evidence is mixed: Clark et al. 2018 found moderate predictive value for some endpoints (rabbit QT post-test odds 83%; LR+ cardiac 3.54; LR+ hepatobiliary 2.8), but Bailey et al. 2015 found absence-of-toxicity in rabbit gave little evidence of safety (median iNLR 1.12).
key_numbers: 83% (rabbit QT post-test odds, Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ 3.54 (rabbit, cardiac disorders, Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ 2.8 (rabbit, hepatobiliary disorders, Clark et al. 2018)
median iNLR 1.12 (rabbit, Bailey et al. 2015)
toxicology|rabbit.why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by endpoint (e.g., QT-specific vs overall selectivity) and by study dataset/selection biases.

toxicology|dog.summary: Evidence is mixed: dogs can predict or exclude some toxicities (LR+ 6.11 for cardiac disorders; 60% post-test odds for QT; Clark et al. 2018) but overall predictive power is modest—median PPV ≈0.67 and NPV ≈0.52 (Atkins et al. 2020). Absence of dog toxicity raised probability of no human toxicity to only ~72% (Bailey et al. 2019); species- and endpoint-specific differences reported (Jang et al. 2019).
key_numbers: median PPV = 0.67 (dog, all grades; Atkins et al. 2020)
median NPV = 0.52 (dog, all grades; Atkins et al. 2020)
72% probability of no human toxicity given no dog toxicity (Bailey et al. 2019)
LR+ = 6.11 for dog cardiac disorders (Clark et al. 2018)
dog iNLR = 1.10 (Bailey et al. 2015)
toxicology|dog.why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by toxicity endpoint, severity and dataset (e.g., cardiac/QT vs subjective 'other' events; Liver‑Chip case studies vs regulatory databases).

toxicology|rat.summary: Evidence is mixed: some metrics show modest rat→human concordance (Jang et al. 2019: 71% of human toxicities predicted by rat+dog testing; Atkins et al. 2020: rat median PPV=0.65; Clark et al. 2018: rat LR+ for cardiac=4.73). However, discrimination is poor for severe toxicities (Atkins PPV grade3–4=0.41) and absence of rat toxicity gives little evidential weight for absence in humans (Bailey et al. 2015: rat iNLR=1.82).
key_numbers: 71% of human toxicities predicted by rat+dog testing (Jang et al. 2019)
Rat median PPV = 0.65 for all toxicity grades (Atkins et al. 2020)
PPV = 0.41 for grade 3–4 toxicities (Atkins et al. 2020)
Rat LR+ for cardiac disorders = 4.73 (Clark et al. 2018)
Rat median iNLR = 1.82 (Bailey et al. 2015)
toxicology|rat.why_range_is_wide: Estimates vary because studies use different metrics (PPV/NPV/LR/iNLR), endpoints and toxicity severities.

toxicology|non-human primate.summary: Evidence is mixed: NHPs can predict some human toxicities (Clark et al. 2018 LR+ 9.52–11.02 for cardiac/hepatobiliary) but overall performance is modest—Monticello et al. 2017 sensitivity 48%, NPV 86%; Atkins et al. 2020 median PPV 0.72, NPV 0.50.
key_numbers: sensitivity 48% (Monticello et al. 2017)
NPV 86% (Monticello et al. 2017)
median PPV 0.72 (Atkins et al. 2020)
median NPV 0.50 (Atkins et al. 2020)
LR+ 9.52–11.02 (Clark et al. 2018, cardiac/hepatobiliary)
toxicology|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by organ system and toxicity grade—some endpoints show high LR+ (cardiac/hepatobiliary) while overall PPVs and sensitivities are much lower; low clinical positive prevalence inflates NPVs.

toxicology|rodent.summary: Rodent toxicology partly tracked human outcomes: sensitivity 48% and PPV 43% for predicting human adverse effects, while specificity 84% and NPV 86% for predicting absence of human AEs. Performance varied by organ (PPV 0%–54%) and rose when rodent+nonrodent shared the same target organ.
key_numbers: Sensitivity 48% (rodent-detected human adverse effects)
PPV 43% (rodent positives that were human adverse effects)
Specificity 84% (rodent negatives matching absence in humans)
NPV 86% (rodent negatives that were absent in humans)
PPV range 0%–54% (ophthalmology to biochemical)
toxicology|rodent.why_range_is_wide: PPV varied by organ system (0% ophthalmology to 54% biochemical) and was higher when the same target organ was identified in both rodent and nonrodent.

toxicology|mouse.summary: Mouse toxicology does not reliably predict human toxicity: Atkins et al. 2020 found median PPV 0.57 (all grades) and 0.43 (grade 3–4) with NPV 0.81 for grade 3–4, and Bailey et al. 2015 reported mouse iNLR 1.39 (≈no evidential weight). Clark et al. 2018 found higher LR+ for some endpoints (cardiac LR+ 5.29; hepatobiliary LR+ 3.73) but no overall statistically significant concordance.
toxicology|mouse.direction: evidence does not favour the model
key_numbers: PPV 0.57 (median, all toxicity grades; Atkins et al. 2020)
PPV 0.43 (median, grade 3–4; Atkins et al. 2020)
NPV 0.81 (median, grade 3–4; Atkins et al. 2020)
LR+ 5.29 (mouse, cardiac disorders; Clark et al. 2018)
iNLR 1.39 (mouse–human median; Bailey et al. 2015)
toxicology|mouse.why_range_is_wide: Concordance varies by toxicity grade and by organ/endpoint (e.g., lower PPV for severe toxicities; higher LR+ for specific cardiac/hepatobiliary endpoints).

toxicology|zebrafish.summary: Evidence shows zebrafish toxicology generally tracks human outcomes: Cornet et al. 2017 found 78% overall accuracy (specificity 89%, sensitivity 68%), Nikam et al. 2020 reported 100% concordance for general/hepatotoxicity and 90% for teratogenicity, and McGrath et al. 2008 found 100% teratogen detection vs 75% non‑teratogen ID. Sensitivity varies by endpoint across studies.
key_numbers: 78% overall accuracy (Cornet et al. 2017)
89% specificity (Cornet et al. 2017)
68% sensitivity (Cornet et al. 2017)
100% concordance for general/hepatotoxicity (Nikam et al. 2020)
100% teratogen detection; 75% non‑teratogen ID (McGrath et al. 2008)
toxicology|zebrafish.why_range_is_wide: Sensitivity differs by toxicity endpoint and platform (e.g. neurotoxicity 54% vs hepatotoxicity 80% in Cornet et al.).

veterinary|dog.summary: Evidence is mixed: dog cancer models show substantial concordance with humans in many cancers (model robustness 31–85% across cancer types; Daluwatumulle et al. 2026), but RPE65 gene therapy outcomes did not translate—dogs had near‑normal ERG while humans showed no sustained ERG improvement (Petersen‑Jones et al. 2015).
key_numbers: 31–85% model robustness scores across cancers (range, Daluwatumulle et al. 2026)
0–24% cancer-specific DEGs across cancers (Daluwatumulle et al. 2026)
mean sample-correlation difference 0.1007 (diff-cancer same-species vs same-cancer diff-species, Daluwatumulle et al. 2026)
1 patient had a transient ERG improvement; others showed no ERG change (Petersen-Jones et al. 2015)
normalized absolute distance per-gene expression 0.007–0.047 between species (Daluwatumulle et al. 2026)
veterinary|dog.why_range_is_wide: Range reflects large variation across cancer types, adult vs pediatric cohorts, and inclusion of positive vs negative control cancers.
veterinary|dog.negative_controls_noted: Negative-control cancers (ACC, LAML) had the lowest scores (≈31–40%).
